chapter: Second session: boyhood, brothers and early road years
title: Special delivery messenger for the Los Angeles post office
summary: On his bicycle he earned eight cents a letter and as much as sixty dollars a month at the main post office at Eighth and Spring.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Oh, I think it must have been about 1900 or 1901 or '2. I don't know. I know that after that I went in the post office as a messenger and that special delivery on my bicycle, and that was about 1902 or '3 or something like that. The old post office then was at Eighth and Spring Street, and...
Was that the post office? Was that the only one?
That was the main post office in those days. and they had all the trucks and things that sent mail out to the other post offices around, and I worked there about two years. I

was doing pretty good. I made about forty, fifty dollars a month. They paid us eight cents a letter, you know. You know a special delivery costs you twelve cents in those days. Ten cents for special delivery and two cents for the postage. So they paid the delivery boy eight cents. Sometime I'd go out with ten or twelve letters at a time and make seventy, eighty cents, come back and make seventy, eighty cents and out again, and sometimes you'd get two, three letters, and you'd have to take you nearly half a day to deliver them because riding your bicycle, you got a letter that was way out here--way out in the country like Western and Adams or something, you... see, you have to pedal all the way out there, pedal all the way back, and you half a day's gone, and maybe you only deliver one letter. But you see your next trip out you mighta get eight or ten letters that you don't go any further than Second and Spring, you know, business places and things. You know, so they tried to equalize, that they can't give you all the stuff downtown and send me out all the time so they you sometime and then they give me sometime I have to go way out. Sometime I have to go way out to Avenue 30 and 40. And you know that's pretty long, pedalling your bicycle and by... We rode free on the streetcars but you didn't always get on a car, and if you was trying to make money, the streetcar was too slow, see? And a lot of us would ride our head off 'cause we could beat the streetcar, which you wouldn't be makin' much on those long trips 'cause generally on the long trips there wasn't but one letter we had to come way out there. Wasn't a gang of letters coming way out there--just maybe one would come.
I used to make forty, fifty dollars a month...sixty dollars a month.
That was pretty good in those times.
Yeah, for a kid, you know. Yeah. Yeah.
So how long did you work for the post office?
